Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 14:30 PT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Marcus Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Daniel Ortiz (Vertex CTO), Sophie Miller (Head of MLOps), Anoop Singh (Data Engineer)
summary: Discovery focused on cost/unit economics for text generation and embeddings. Customer has a mid-market fintech workload with interactive prompts and batch embedding jobs. Key concerns: per-token cost, latency SLOs (~<200ms for interactive), caching and batching levers, privacy/data residency. Redwood to run benchmarks and send pricing/security docs. Potential interest in Dedicated if cost and latency targets require reserved capacity.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
Quantization and model variants impact on cost
transcript:
[00:00] Marcus (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Marcus, AE on the account, and Priya's our solutions engineer. Quick intros?
[00:12] Daniel (Vertex CTO): Daniel here, CTO. Sophie runs MLOps, and Anoop is our lead data engineer.
[00:20] Priya (Redwood SE): Nice to meet you all. Today Marcos — Marcus — wants to focus on cost per token and levers you can pull to meet a budget.
[00:30] Marcus: Yeah, exactly. We know a lot of teams hit questions around economics: hosted per-token pricing, batching/caching, dedicated pricing, and what a private deploy looks like if you have compliance constraints.
[01:05] Sophie: To give context, our app is an analyst-facing assistant. Typical interactive session is 800–1,200 tokens per request, sometimes longer, and we also run nightly embedding jobs for vectors at ~1M rows per month. Budget-wise, preliminary cap is around $10k–$20k per month but we need to be careful, and latency for in-product responses needs to feel near real-time — under ~200–300ms ideally.
[01:40] Marcus: Got it. That combination — high tokens per request and a mix of large embedding batches — is exactly where batching and caching can matter. Quick question: are you currently using any managed LLM API?
[01:55] Daniel: We're prototyping with OpenAI for generation and using a smaller self-hosted for embeddings, but cost for generation at scale is a concern and data residency is also on the checklist.
[02:10] Priya: Makes sense. I'll walk through the primary levers: model choice, batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization/model variants, and then deployment mode — hosted vs Dedicated vs Private — which changes unit economics and SLOs.
[02:35] [02:35] Priya: First, per-token pricing — on Redwood Hosted we price per input and output token. Higher-capacity models cost more per token but often reduce prompt-engineering overhead. For illustration, a smaller open model might be 0.6x cost but slower or lower quality; larger model 1.5–2x cost but better quality.
[03:05] Sophie: Do you have worked examples? Like for a 1,000-token roundtrip how the cost stacks up?
[03:12] Marcus: Yes, we'll send a pricing sheet. But rough calc here: if a given hosted model is $0.0008 per input token and $0.0012 per output token, a 1,000 token roundtrip is ~ $2.0. If you do 5k sessions/day that's $10k/day, so obviously scale matters.
[03:38] [03:38] Anoop: Wait — those numbers scale fast. We're not at 5k sessions yet; maybe 2k sessions/day peak. But embeddings at 1M rows, even at $0.0002 per embedding unit, add up.
[03:52] Priya: Right — two immediate levers to reduce per-unit cost: batching and caching. With batching you can amortize GPU compute across multiple requests; for throughput-oriented workloads this reduces per-token CPU/GPU time. Caching, especially prefix/KV caching, avoids recomputing the prefix attentions for repeated prompts.
[04:20] [04:20] Priya: Example: for interactive sessions with repeated system prompts or templates, prefix caching can reduce compute 20–60% depending on prompt reuse. For embeddings you can run large batch jobs off-peak and apply quantized models to lower cost.
[04:38] Daniel: How does batching affect latency? If we batch to achieve cost savings, does that introduce queuing delay unacceptable for the <200ms SLO?
[04:48] Priya: Good question. Batching is a tradeoff. For strict latency SLOs, Redwood can be configured to use small continuous batches with tight latency targets — e.g., 1–5ms additional queuing for interactive flows — but you pay less from batching at high concurrency. If your 200ms SLO is firm, we often recommend Dedicated reserved pools sized for your peak to avoid queuing.
[05:15] Marcus: Also, we can set routing policy per route: interactive route pinned to low-latency Dedicated instance, while background embedding jobs go to cheaper preemptible capacity or scheduled batches.
[05:34] [05:34] Sophie: That routing split sounds promising. If we moved interactive to Dedicated, what's the typical committed spend?
[05:43] Priya: Dedicated pricing is based on reserved GPU capacity. For a small Dedicated pool that meets 200ms for your workload you might be looking at a monthly committed spend in the ballpark of $10k–$25k depending on model and concurrency. The delta vs hosted is you get predictable throughput and better per-token unit economics at scale.
[06:05] Anoop: Does Dedicated come with isolated KV cache and no multi-tenant interference?
[06:10] Priya: Yes, Dedicated gives you isolated pools and data isolation; KV cache lives in your capacity and isn't shared. For extra guarantees around network and control we have the Private deployment (VPC or on-prem) option.
[06:22] [06:22] Daniel: For Private, how different is the pricing — is it an upfront license plus infra?
[06:27] Marcus: Private typically includes a platform fee plus infra and support. For customers who need on-prem or air-gapped, it's more of an enterprise engagement and costs are higher due to ops/support, but it addresses compliance/residency.
[06:41] Sophie: Back to per-token math — can Redwood show us how batching + quantization + caching would change our $/request?
[06:50] Priya: Absolutely. In the benchmark we run your representative prompts, with your concurrency profile. We test variants: hosted large model, hosted quantized variant, Dedicated with 4-bit quantization, and also caching enabled. Typically you might see 30–60% cost reduction using quantized variants plus caching, depending on quality tolerance.
[07:15] [07:15] Daniel: Quality tolerance — would quantized models degrade outputs for our analyst use? We're sensitive to hallucinations.
[07:22] Priya: There's always a tradeoff. We recommend running evals on your prompt set as part of the benchmark. Often 4-bit quantized variants hold up well for many tasks; we track per-prompt quality regressions and can recommend the minimal model that meets your quality bar.
[07:40] Marcus: We'll include evaluation criteria in the benchmark plan so you can see side-by-side exact differences on your prompts.
[07:51] [07:51] Anoop: For embeddings, is there an internal dedupe or cache strategy? We re-run many similar rows during updates.
[07:58] Priya: For embeddings we offer de-dup caches and vector dedupe tooling; plus batching large embedding jobs overnight reduces cost. Also you can use a slightly smaller embedding model for near-similarity and then only re-embed changed rows.
[08:12] Sophie: Our compliance folks will ask about encryption and KMS. Do you support customer-managed keys for logs and model inputs?
[08:20] Marcus: Yes, for Dedicated and Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key management. Hosted supports encryption at rest and in transit; customer-managed keys are available on Dedicated/private options. SOC 2 and ISO docs we'll send over.
[08:36] [08:36] Daniel: How do you instrument cost per route? We want to show product teams how much a particular prompt costs.
[08:43] Priya: Redwood Console provides token-level breakdowns per-route and per-model. You can attribute cost to API keys, endpoints, or users; that helps create internal chargebacks.
[08:54] Marcus: We can also produce a per-prompt cost example you can dump into your internal chargeback dashboard.
[09:03] [09:03] Sophie: Ok, two quick scenario questions: 1) If we stay hosted and scale to 200k sessions/month, what's your best-in-class per-token cost? 2) If we commit to Dedicated, how much would per-token drop?
[09:18] Priya: Rough rough answers — hosted per-token might be X baseline; let me be concrete: imagine hosted model cost $0.0008 in/ $0.0012 out. With good batching/caching you could lower effective cost by 25–40% depending on reuse. With Dedicated plus quantized models, another 20–40% reduction is possible. We'll put real numbers in the pricing sheet and benchmark results because it depends on sequence lengths and reuse.
[09:50] [09:50] Anoop: Do you support mixed routing in a single API so we don't have to change client code?
[09:55] Marcus: Yes — routes in the Redwood API can be configured to hit different backends transparently; we can keep the same API surface.
[10:05] Sophie: For your benchmarks, what data do you need from us?
[10:09] Priya: We need a representative sample of prompts (including system prompts), distribution of token lengths, concurrency profile (peak QPS), and some embedding sample rows. Also quality evaluation criteria — what counts as acceptable.
[10:22] [10:22] Daniel: We can provide a 200-prompt sample and a 10k-row embedding sample to start.
[10:27] Marcus: Perfect. We'll schedule the benchmark and share the plan.
[10:33] [10:33] Sophie: Any limitations on model variants for Dedicated — e.g., can we run a custom fine-tuned model?
[10:39] Priya: Dedicated supports pinned model versions and you can bring your own fine-tuned model subject to some Ops constraints — we'll detail that in the engagement doc. For Private/on-prem it's more flexible.
[10:54] [10:54] Anoop: How do burst scenarios work? If we get sudden traffic spikes, do you auto-scale?
[10:58] Marcus: For Hosted we have autoscaling but it's multi-tenant; Dedicated has configurable autoscaling policies and optional burst capacity. We can size for steady plus burst.
[11:12] Sophie: One of our stakeholders asked about token accounting for tool-calling and function outputs — is that treated as output tokens?
[11:19] Priya: Yes, everything returned by the model counts as output tokens. For function/tool calls we can sometimes compress outputs or use structured responses to reduce token overhead.
[11:30] [11:30] Daniel: Any real customer examples of cost savings after moving to Dedicated?
[11:35] Marcus: We have a mid-market fintech that moved their interactive route to Dedicated and saw ~35% reduction in per-interaction cost while improving p95 latency from 320ms to 180ms. We'll anonymize and include that case study.
[11:50] [11:50] Sophie: Sounds good. Let's talk pricing cadence: do you do monthly snapshots or annual committed discounts?
[11:57] Marcus: Both. Dedicated typically comes with enterprise tiers and annual commitments for additional discounts. Hosted has volume tiers that reduce per-token rates at scale.
[12:10] [12:10] Anoop: On the technical side, what's the KV cache TTL and invalidation patterns? We update system prompts occasionally.
[12:18] Priya: TTLs are configurable per-route. You can invalidate prefixes on deploy or set short TTLs for dynamic content. For large reuse we keep a longer TTL.
[12:32] [12:32] Daniel: Any thought on hybrid where embeddings stay in our VPC but generation is hosted?
[12:38] Marcus: Yes, hybrid is common: keep sensitive data and embeddings on Private or Dedicated in your VPC while using Hosted for non-sensitive generation. We can route per model/endpoint accordingly.
[12:52] Sophie: Ok, let's summarize next steps.
[12:56] Marcus: Recap — 1) We'll send pricing sheet and worked examples. 2) Priya will propose benchmark slots; we run a 2-hour benchmark with your prompts and compare hosted/quantized/dedicated. 3) Send SOC2/ISO and Private deployment guide. 4) Sophie will provide volume estimates and latency SLOs.
[13:20] [13:20] Daniel: One last thought — if the Dedicated committed spend is slightly above our current budget but yields better predictability and lower per-token, how flexible are commit sizes?
[13:31] Priya: We can size commits conservatively and add burst capacity or short-term top-ups while you ramp. There's flexibility in the commercial terms.
[13:45] Marcus: Great. We'll follow up on dates and files. Thanks everyone.
[13:50] Daniel: Thanks.
[13:52] Sophie: Thanks, bye.
[46:00] [call ended]
